3475: #### 3. Transport architecture
3476: 
3477: The Bluetooth data transport system follows a layered architecture. This description of the Bluetooth system describes the Bluetooth core transport layers up to and including L2CAP channels. All Bluetooth operational modes follow the same generic transport architecture, which is shown in [Figure 3.1](architecture.html#UUID-3189feb9-4465-ee4a-d054-c1cbd98f3e3f_figure-idm4568343564201633540292615318 "Figure 3.1: Bluetooth generic data transport architecture").
3478: 
3479: ![Bluetooth generic data transport architecture](../image/img-7db79712c93d681c79b67781d243f280.png)
3480: 
3481: Figure 3.1: Bluetooth generic data transport architecture
3482: 
3483:   
3484:   
3485: 
3486: For efficiency and legacy reasons, the Bluetooth transport architecture includes a sub-division of the logical layer, distinguishing between logical links and logical transports. This sub-division provides a general (and commonly understood) concept of a logical link that provides an independent transport between two or more devices. The logical transport sub-layer is required to describe the inter-dependence between some of the logical link types (mainly for reasons of legacy behavior).
3487: 
3488: The ACL, SCO, and eSCO connections are considered as logical transports but often behave as separate physical links. However, they are not as independent as might be desired, due to their shared use of resources such as the LT\_ADDR and acknowledgment/repeat request (ARQ) scheme. Hence the architecture is incapable of representing these logical transports with a single transport layer. The additional logical transport layer goes some way towards describing this behavior.
3489: 
3490: ##### 3.1. Core traffic bearers
3491: 
3492: The Bluetooth core system provides a number of standard traffic bearers for the transport of service protocol and application data. These are shown in [Figure 3.2](architecture.html#UUID-eed29331-57a3-2de7-c147-bd2fa23add03_figure-idm4642746768408033541876932625 "Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers") below (for ease of representation this is shown with higher layers to the left and lower layers to the right).
3493: 
3494: ![Bluetooth traffic bearers](../image/img-72b45c5848b218c7c67eed25df832a27.png)
3495: 
3496: Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers
3497: 
3498:   
3499:   
3500: 
3501: The core traffic bearers that are available to applications are shown in [Figure 3.2](architecture.html#UUID-eed29331-57a3-2de7-c147-bd2fa23add03_figure-idm4642746768408033541876932625 "Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers") as the shaded rounded rectangles. The architectural layers that are defined to provide these services are described in [Section 2](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e "2 Core system architecture"). A number of data traffic types are shown on the left of the diagram linked to the traffic bearers that are typically suitable for transporting that type of data traffic.
3502: 
3503: The logical links are named using the names of the associated logical transport and a suffix that indicates the type of data that is transported. (C for control links carrying LMP or LL messages, U for L2CAP links carrying user data (L2CAP PDUs) and S for stream links carrying unformatted synchronous or isochronous data.) It is common for the suffix to be removed from the logical link without introducing ambiguity, thus a reference to the default ACL logical transport can be resolved to mean the ACL-C logical link in cases where the LMP protocol is being discussed, the LE-C logical link in cases where LL protocol is being discussed, or the ACL-U or LE-U logical links when the L2CAP layer is being discussed.
3504: 
3505: The mapping of application traffic types to Bluetooth core traffic bearers in [Figure 3.2](architecture.html#UUID-eed29331-57a3-2de7-c147-bd2fa23add03_figure-idm4642746768408033541876932625 "Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers") is based on matching the traffic characteristics with the bearer characteristics. It is recommended to use these mappings as they provide the most natural and efficient method of transporting the data with its given characteristics.
3506: 
3507: However, an application (or an implementation of the Bluetooth core system) may choose to use a different traffic bearer, or a different mapping to achieve a similar result. For example, in a BR/EDR piconet with only one Peripheral, the Central may choose to transport L2CAP broadcasts over the ACL-U logical link rather than over the APB-U logical link. This will probably be more efficient in terms of bandwidth (if the physical channel quality is not too degraded). Use of alternative transport paths to those in [Figure 3.2](architecture.html#UUID-eed29331-57a3-2de7-c147-bd2fa23add03_figure-idm4642746768408033541876932625 "Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers") is only acceptable if the characteristics of the application traffic type are preserved.
3508: 
3509: [Figure 3.2](architecture.html#UUID-eed29331-57a3-2de7-c147-bd2fa23add03_figure-idm4642746768408033541876932625 "Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers") shows a number of application traffic types. These are used to classify the types of data that may be submitted to the Bluetooth core system. The original data traffic type can be different from the type that is submitted to the Bluetooth core system if an intervening process modifies it. For example, video data is generated at a constant rate but an intermediate coding process may alter this to variable rate, e.g. by MPEG4 encoding. For the purposes of the Bluetooth core system, only the characteristic of the submitted data is of interest.
3510: 
3511: ###### 3.1.1. Framed data traffic
3512: 
3513: The L2CAP layer services provide a frame-oriented transport for asynchronous and isochronous user data. The application submits data to this service in variable-sized frames (up to a negotiated maximum for the channel) and these frames are delivered in the same form to the corresponding application on the remote device. There is no requirement for the application to insert additional framing information into the data, although it may do so if this is required (such framing is invisible to the Bluetooth core system).
3514: 
3515: Connection-oriented L2CAP channels may be created for transport of unicast (point-to-point) data between two Bluetooth devices. Connection-oriented channels provide a context within which specific properties may be applied to data transported on the channel. For example, quality of service parameters or flow and error control modes may be applied. Connection-oriented L2CAP channels are created using the L2CAP connection procedure.
3516: 
3517: A connectionless BR/EDR L2CAP channel exists for broadcasting data or for transport of unicast data. In the case of piconet topologies the Central is always the source of broadcast data and the Peripheral(s) are the recipients. Broadcast traffic on the connectionless L2CAP channel is uni-directional. Unicast data sent on the connectionless L2CAP channels may be uni-directional or bi-directional. Unicast data sent on the L2CAP connectionless channel provides an alternate mechanism to send data with the same level of reliability as an L2CAP connection-oriented channel operating in Basic mode but without the additional latency incurred by opening an L2CAP connection-oriented channel. LE L2CAP connectionless channels are not supported.
3518: 
3519: BR/EDR L2CAP channels have an associated QoS setting that defines constraints on the delivery of the frames of data. These QoS settings may be used to indicate (for example) that the data is isochronous, and therefore has a limited lifetime after which it becomes invalid, or that the data should be delivered within a given time period, or that the data is reliable and should be delivered without error, however long this takes.
3520: 
3521: Some L2CAP channels are fixed channels created when the ACL-U and/or LE-U logical links are established. These fixed channels have fixed channel identifiers and fixed configurations and do not permit negotiation of the configuration after they are created. These fixed channels are used for BR/EDR and LE L2CAP signaling (ACL-U or LE-U), connectionless channel (ACL-U and APB-U), Security Manager Protocol (LE-U), and Attribute Protocol (ACL-U or LE-U).
3522: 
3523: The L2CAP channel manager is responsible for arranging to transport the L2CAP channel data frames on an appropriate baseband logical link, possibly multiplexing this onto the baseband logical link with other L2CAP channels with similar characteristics.
3524: 
3525: ###### 3.1.2. Unframed data traffic
3526: 
3527: If the application does not require delivery of data in frames, possibly because it includes in-stream framing, or because the data is a pure stream, then it may avoid the use of L2CAP channels and make direct use of a baseband logical link.
3528: 
3529: The Bluetooth core system supports the direct transport of application data that is isochronous and of a constant rate (either bit-rate, or frame-rate for pre-framed data), using a SCO-S or eSCO-S logical link. These logical links reserve physical channel bandwidth and provide a constant rate transport locked to the piconet clock. Data is transported in fixed size packets at fixed intervals with both of these parameters negotiated during channel establishment. eSCO links provide a greater choice of bit-rates and also provide greater reliability by using limited retransmission in case of error. Enhanced Data Rate operation is supported for eSCO, but not for SCO logical transports. SCO and eSCO logical transports do not support multiplexed logical links or any further layering within the Bluetooth core. An application may choose to layer a number of streams within the submitted SCO/eSCO stream, provided that the submitted stream is, or has the appearance of being, a constant rate stream.
3530: 
3531: The Bluetooth core system also supports the direct transport of application data using a Profile Broadcast Data (PBD) logical link. This logical link is similar to SCO-S and eSCO-S since it reserves physical channel bandwidth, provides a constant rate transport locked to the piconet clock, and transports data at fixed intervals. It does not support multiplexed logical links or any further layering within the Bluetooth core but, unlike SCO-S and eSCO-S, it supports broadcasting data from a single transmitter to many receivers.
3532: 
3533: The application chooses the most appropriate type of logical link from those available at the baseband, and creates and configures it to transport the data stream, and releases it when completed. (The application will normally also use a framed L2CAP unicast channel to transport its C-plane information to the peer application on the remote device.)
3534: 
3535: If the application data is isochronous and of a variable rate, then this may only be carried by the L2CAP unicast channel, and hence will be treated as framed data.
3536: 
3537: Unframed data traffic is not supported in the LE system.
3538: 
3539: ###### 3.1.3. Reliability of traffic bearers
3540: 
3541: A link or channel is characterized as reliable if the receiver is capable of detecting errors in received packets and requesting retransmission until the errors are removed. This is known as an Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) scheme. Due to the error detection systems used, some residual undetected errors may still remain in the received data. The rate at which these occur depends on the details of the error detection system.
3542: 
3543: A link or channel is characterized as unreliable if the receiver is not capable of detecting errors in received packets or if it can detect errors but cannot request retransmission. In the latter case (such as with most broadcast links), the packets passed on by the receiver to higher layers may be without error but there is no guarantee that all the packets that were sent are received. Uses for unreliable links are normally dependent on techniques to improve the redundancy of the transmission, such as the use of Forward Error Connection or the repetition of data from the higher layers while the data is valid, in order to increase the probability that the receiver is able to receive at least one of the copies successfully.
3544: 
3545: ###### 3.1.3.1. BR/EDR reliability
3546: 
3547: Bluetooth is a wireless communications system. In poor RF environments, this system should be considered inherently unreliable. To counteract this the system provides levels of protection at each layer. The baseband packet header uses forward error correcting (FEC) coding to allow error correction by the receiver and a header error check (HEC) to detect errors remaining after correction. Certain Baseband packet types include FEC for the payload. Furthermore, some Baseband packet types include a cyclic redundancy error check (CRC).
3548: 
3549: On ACL logical transports the results of the error detection algorithm are used to drive a simple ARQ protocol. This provides an enhanced reliability by re-transmitting packets that do not pass the receiver’s error checking algorithm. It is possible to modify this scheme to support latency-sensitive packets by discarding an unsuccessfully transmitted packet at the transmitter if the packet’s useful life has expired. eSCO links use a modified version of this scheme to improve reliability by allowing a limited number of retransmissions.
3550: 
3551: The resulting reliability gained by this ARQ scheme is only as dependable as the ability of the HEC and CRC codes to detect errors. In most cases this is sufficient, however it has been shown that for the longer packet types the probability of an undetected error is too high to support typical applications, especially those with a large amount of data being transferred.
3552: 
3553: The L2CAP layer provides an additional level of error control that is designed to detect the occasional errors not detected by the baseband and request retransmission of the affected data. This provides the level of reliability required by typical Bluetooth applications. The resulting rate of residual errors is comparable to the rate in other communication systems.
3554: 
3555: The transmitter may remove packets from the transmit queue such that the receiver does not receive all the packets in the sequence. If this happens detection of the missing packets is delegated to the L2CAP layer.
3556: 
3557: Stream links have a reliability characteristic somewhere between a reliable and an unreliable link, depending on the current operating conditions.
3558: 
3559: ###### 3.1.3.2. LE reliability
3560: 
3561: Like BR/EDR, in poor RF environments, the LE system should be considered inherently unreliable. To counteract this, the system provides levels of protection at each layer. The LL packet uses a 24-bit cyclic redundancy error check (CRC) to cover the contents of the packet payload. If the CRC verification fails on the packet payload, the packet is not acknowledged by the receiver and the packet gets retransmitted by the sender.
3562: 
3563: Because of the longer CRC and the shorter typical message compared with BR/EDR, it is not necessary for the L2CAP layer to provide a separate error detection and retransmission mechanism.

3567: ##### 3.2. Transport architecture entities
3568: 
3569: The Bluetooth transport architecture entities are shown in [Figure 3.3](architecture.html#UUID-b056a5a6-13d3-3970-a024-a744a3b59127_figure-idm4568346290993633540305876435 "Figure 3.3: Overview of transport architecture entities and hierarchy ") and are described from the lowest layer upwards in the subsequent sections.

3578: The BR/EDR Physical Transport encapsulates the BR/EDR Physical Channels. Transfers using the BR/EDR Physical Transport use the BR/EDR Generic Packet Structure. The LE Physical Transport encapsulates the LE Physical Channels. Transfers using the LE Physical Transport use the LE Generic Packet Structure for transferring user data and LL control information. The LE Physical Transport is also used for transfers using the Channel Sounding generic packet structure and signaling format.

3580: ###### 3.2.1. BR/EDR generic packet structure
3581: 
3582: The generic packet structure nearly reflects the architectural layers found in the Bluetooth BR/EDR system. The BR/EDR packet structure is designed for optimal use in normal operation. It is shown in [Figure 3.4](architecture.html#UUID-1a6ed991-87a6-8dbd-710d-d1422a350644_figure-idm4543874365804833540310285772 "Figure 3.4: BR/EDR packet structure").
3583: 
3584: ![BR/EDR packet structure](../image/img-2b6a8b6697a072aa86bdf7f7bf905cbf.png)
3585: 
3586: Figure 3.4: BR/EDR packet structure
3587: 
3588:   
3589:   
3590: 
3591: Packets normally only include the fields that are necessary to represent the layers required by the transaction. Thus a simple inquiry request over an inquiry scan physical channel does not create or require a logical link or higher layer and therefore consists only of the channel access code (associated with the physical channel).
3592: 
3593: All packets include the channel access code. This is used to identify communications on a particular physical channel and therefore ignore packets on a different physical channel that happens to be using the same RF carrier in physical proximity.
3594: 
3595: There is no direct field within the BR/EDR packet structure that represents or contains information relating to physical links. This information is implied by the combination of the logical transport address (LT\_ADDR) carried in the packet header and the channel access code (CAC).
3596: 
3597: Most BR/EDR packets include a packet header. The packet header is always present in packets transmitted on physical channels that support physical links, logical transports and logical links. The packet header carries the LT\_ADDR, which is used by each receiving device to determine if the packet is addressed to the device and is used to route the packet internally.
3598: 
3599: The BR/EDR packet header also carries part of the link control (LC) protocol that is operated per logical transport (except for ACL and SCO transports that operate a shared LC protocol carried on either logical transport).
3600: 
3601: The Enhanced Data Rate (EDR) packets have a guard time and synchronization sequence before the payload. This is a field used for physical layer change of modulation scheme.
3602: 
3603: The payload header is present in all packets on logical transports that support multiple logical links. The payload header includes a logical link identifier field used for routing the payload, and a field indicating the length of the payload body. Some packet types also include a CRC at the end of the packet payload that is used to detect most errors in received packets. When AES-CCM encryption is enabled, ACL packets include a Message Integrity Check (MIC) just prior to the CRC.
3604: 
3605: EDR packets have a trailer after the CRC.
3606: 
3607: The packet payload body is used to transport the user data. The interpretation of this data is dependent on the logical transport and logical link identifiers. For ACL logical transports Link Manager protocol (LMP) messages and L2CAP signals are transported in the packet payload body, along with general user data from applications.
3608: 
3609: For SCO, eSCO, and CPB logical transports the payload body contains the user data for the logical link.
3610: 
3611: ###### 3.2.2. LE generic packet structure
3612: 
3613: LE radio operation is based on four PHYs and makes use of two modulation symbol rates. [Table 3.1](architecture.html#UUID-68615d2c-776f-f78d-1f4f-5b514754f641_table-idm13358695537488 "Table 3.1: Summary of PHYs, modulation schemes, and coding schemes") summarizes the properties of each of the LE PHYs. Each packet transmitted uses a single PHY. Three of the PHYs are uncoded - that is, each bit maps directly to a single radio symbol in the packet - while the fourth PHY is error correction coded. There are two coding schemes: S=8 and S=2, where S is the number of symbols per bit.

3876: ##### 3.3. Physical channels
3877: 
3878: A number of types of physical channel are defined. All Bluetooth physical channels are characterized by a set of PHY frequencies combined with temporal parameters and restricted by spatial considerations. For the basic and adapted piconet physical channels frequency hopping is used to change frequency periodically to reduce the effects of interference and for regulatory reasons.
3879: 
3880: The Bluetooth BR/EDR system and LE system differ slightly in the way they use physical channels.
3881: 
3882: ###### 3.3.1. BR/EDR physical channels
3883: 
3884: In the BR/EDR core system, peer devices use a shared physical channel for communication. To achieve this their transceivers need to be tuned to the same PHY frequency at the same time, and they need to be within a nominal range of each other.
3885: 
3886: Given that the number of RF carriers is limited and that many Bluetooth devices may be operating independently within the same spatial and temporal area there is a strong likelihood of two independent Bluetooth devices having their transceivers tuned to the same RF carrier, resulting in a physical channel collision. To mitigate the unwanted effects of this collision each transmission on a physical channel starts with an access code that is used as a correlation code by devices tuned to the physical channel. This channel access code is a property of the physical channel. The access code is present at the start of every transmitted packet.
3887: 
3888: Several BR/EDR physical channels are defined. Each is optimized and used for a different purpose. Two of these physical channels (the basic piconet channel and adapted piconet channel) are used for communication between connected devices and are associated with a specific piconet. Other BR/EDR physical channels are used for discovering (the inquiry scan channel) and connecting (the page scan channel) Bluetooth devices. The synchronization scan physical channel is used by devices to obtain timing and frequency information about the Connectionless Peripheral Broadcast physical link or to recover the current piconet clock.
3889: 
3890: A Bluetooth device can only use one BR/EDR physical channel at any given time. In order to support multiple concurrent operations the device uses time-division multiplexing between the channels. In this way a Bluetooth device can appear to operate simultaneously in several piconets, as well as being discoverable and connectable.
3891: 
3892: Whenever a Bluetooth device is synchronized to the timing, frequency and access code of a physical channel it is said to be ‘connected’ to this channel (whether or not it is actively involved in communications over the channel). The Bluetooth specification assumes that a device is only capable of connecting to one physical channel at any time. Advanced devices may be capable of connecting simultaneously to more than one physical channel, but the specification does not assume that this is possible.
3893: 
3894: ###### 3.3.1.1. Basic piconet channel
3895: 
3896: ###### 3.3.1.1.1. Overview
3897: 
3898: The basic piconet channel is used for communication between connected devices during normal operation.
3899: 
3900: ###### 3.3.1.1.2. Characteristics
3901: 
3902: The basic piconet channel is characterized by a pseudo-random sequence hopping through the PHY channels. The hopping sequence is unique for the piconet and is determined by the Bluetooth Device Address of the Central. The phase in the hopping sequence is determined by the Bluetooth clock of the Central. All Bluetooth devices participating in the piconet are time- and hop-synchronized to the channel.
3903: 
3904: The channel is divided into time slots where each slot corresponds to an PHY hop frequency. Consecutive hops correspond to different PHY hop frequencies. The time slots are numbered according to the Bluetooth clock of the piconet Central. Packets are transmitted by Bluetooth devices participating in the piconet aligned to start at a slot boundary. Each packet starts with the channel access code, which is derived from the Bluetooth Device Address of the piconet Central.
3905: 
3906: On the basic piconet channel the Central controls access to the channel. The Central starts its transmission in even-numbered time slots only. Packets transmitted by the Central are aligned with the slot start and define the piconet timing. Packets transmitted by the Central may occupy up to five time slots depending on the packet type.
3907: 
3908: Each Central transmission is a packet carrying information on one of the logical transports. Peripherals may transmit on the physical channel in response. The characteristics of the response are defined by the logical transport that is addressed.
3909: 
3910: For example, on the asynchronous connection-oriented logical transport (ACL), the addressed Peripheral responds by transmitting a packet containing information for the same logical transport that is nominally aligned with the next (odd-numbered) slot start. Such a packet may occupy up to five time slots, depending on the packet type. On a broadcast logical transport no Peripherals are allowed to respond.
3911: 
3912: ###### 3.3.1.1.3. Topology
3913: 
3914: A basic piconet channel may be shared by any number of Bluetooth devices, limited only by the resources available on the piconet Central. Only one device is the piconet Central, all others being piconet Peripherals. All communication is between the Central and Peripherals. There is no direct communication between Peripherals on the piconet channel.
3915: 
3916: There is, however, a limitation on the number of logical transports that can be supported within a piconet. This means that although there is no theoretical limit to the number of Bluetooth devices that share a channel there is a limit to the number of these devices that can be actively involved in exchanging data with the Central.
3917: 
3918: ###### 3.3.1.1.4. Supported layers
3919: 
3920: The basic piconet channel supports a number of physical links, logical transports, logical links and L2CAP channels used for general purpose communications.
3921: 
3922: ###### 3.3.1.2. Adapted piconet channel
3923: 
3924: ###### 3.3.1.2.1. Overview
3925: 
3926: The adapted piconet channel differs from the basic piconet channel in two ways. First, the frequency on which a Peripheral transmits is the same as the frequency used by its Central in the preceding transmission. In other words the frequency is not recomputed between Central and subsequent Peripheral packets. Second, the adapted piconet channel may be based on fewer than the full 79 frequencies. A number of frequencies may be omitted from the hopping pattern by being marked as “unused”. The remainder of the 79 frequencies are included. The two sequences are the same except that whenever the basic pseudo-random hopping sequence selects an unused frequency, it is replaced with an alternative chosen from the used set. The set of frequencies used may vary between different physical links on the same adapted piconet channel.
3927: 
3928: Because the adapted piconet channel uses the same timing and access code as the basic piconet channel, physical links on the two channels are often coincident. This provides a deliberate benefit as it allows Peripherals in either the basic piconet channel or the adapted piconet channel to adjust their synchronization to the Central.
3929: 
3930: The topology and supported layers of the adapted piconet physical channel are identical to the basic piconet physical channel with one exception: on the adapted piconet physical channel, it is possible for a single Central to transmit data to an unlimited number of Peripherals using a single CPB logical transport. In this case, however, data is only transferred from Central to Peripheral and not from Peripheral to Central.
3931: 
3932: ###### 3.3.1.3. Inquiry scan channel
3933: 
3934: ###### 3.3.1.3.1. Overview
3935: 
3936: In order for a device to be discovered, an inquiry scan channel is used. A discoverable device listens for inquiry requests on its inquiry scan channel and then sends a response to that request. In order for a device to discover other devices, it iterates (hops) through all possible inquiry scan channel frequencies in a pseudo-random fashion, sending an inquiry request on each frequency and listening for any response.
3937: 
3938: ###### 3.3.1.3.2. Characteristics
3939: 
3940: Inquiry scan channels follow a slower hopping pattern and use an access code to distinguish between occasional occupancy of the same radio frequency by two co-located devices using different physical channels.
3941: 
3942: The access code used on the inquiry scan channel is taken from a reserved set of inquiry access codes that are shared by all Bluetooth devices. One access code is used for general inquiries, and a number of additional access codes are reserved for limited inquiries. Each device has access to a number of different inquiry scan channels. As all of these channels share an identical hopping pattern, a device may concurrently occupy more than one inquiry scan channel if it is capable of concurrently correlating more than one access code.
3943: 
3944: A device using one of its inquiry scan channels remains passive on that channel until it receives an inquiry message on this channel from another Bluetooth device. This is identified by the appropriate inquiry access code. The inquiry scanning device will then follow the inquiry response procedure to return a response to the inquiring device.
3945: 
3946: In order for a device to discover other Bluetooth devices it uses the inquiry scan channel to send inquiry requests. As it has no prior knowledge of the devices to discover, it cannot know the exact characteristics of the inquiry scan channel.
3947: 
3948: The device takes advantage of the fact that inquiry scan channels have a reduced number of hop frequencies and a slower rate of hopping. The inquiring device transmits inquiry requests on each of the inquiry scan hop frequencies and listens for an inquiry response. Transmissions are done at a faster rate, allowing the inquiring device to cover all inquiry scan frequencies in a reasonably short time period.
3949: 
3950: ###### 3.3.1.3.3. Topology
3951: 
3952: Inquiring and discoverable devices use a simple exchange of packets to fulfill the inquiring function. The topology formed during this transaction is a simple and transient point-to-point connection.
3953: 
3954: ###### 3.3.1.3.4. Supported layers
3955: 
3956: During the exchange of packets between an inquiring and discoverable device it may be considered that a temporary physical link exists between these devices. However, the concept is quite irrelevant as it has no physical representation but is only implied by the brief transaction between the devices. No further architectural layers are considered to be supported.
3957: 
3958: ###### 3.3.1.4. Page scan channel
3959: 
3960: ###### 3.3.1.4.1. Overview
3961: 
3962: A connectable device (one that is prepared to accept connections) does so using a page scan channel. A connectable device listens for a page request on its page scan channel and, once received, enters into a sequence of exchanges with this device. In order for a device to connect to another device, it iterates (hops) through all page scan channel frequencies in a pseudo-random fashion, sending a page request on each frequency and listening for a response.
3963: 
3964: ###### 3.3.1.4.2. Characteristics
3965: 
3966: The page scan channel uses an access code derived from the scanning device’s Bluetooth Device Address to identify communications on the channel. The page scan channel uses a slower hopping rate than the hop rate of the basic and adapted piconet channels. The hop selection algorithm uses the Bluetooth device clock of the scanning device as an input.
3967: 
3968: A device using its page scan channel remains passive until it receives a page request from another Bluetooth device. This is identified by the page scan channel access code. The two devices will then follow the page procedure to form a connection. Following a successful conclusion of the page procedure both devices switch to the basic piconet channel that is characterized by having the paging device as Central.
3969: 
3970: In order for a device to connect to another Bluetooth device it uses the page scan channel of the target device in order to send page requests. If the paging device does not know the phase of the target device’s page scan channel it therefore does not know the current hop frequency of the target device. The paging device transmits page requests on each of the page scan hop frequencies and listens for a page response. This is done at a faster hop rate, allowing the paging device to cover all page scan frequencies in a reasonably short time period.
3971: 
3972: The paging device may have some knowledge of the target device’s Bluetooth clock (indicated during a previous inquiry transaction between the two devices, or as a result of a previous involvement in a piconet with the device), in this case it is able to predict the phase of the target device’s page scan channel. It may use this information to optimize the synchronization of the paging and page scanning process and speed up the formation of the connection.
3973: 
3974: ###### 3.3.1.4.3. Topology
3975: 
3976: Paging and connectable devices use a simple exchange of packets to fulfill the paging function. The topology formed during this transaction is a simple and transient point-to-point connection.
3977: 
3978: ###### 3.3.1.4.4. Supported layers
3979: 
3980: During the exchange of packets between a paging and connectable device it may be considered that a temporary physical link exists between these devices. However, the concept is quite irrelevant as it has no physical representation but is only implied by the brief transaction between the devices. No further architectural layers are considered to be supported.
3981: 
3982: ###### 3.3.1.5. Synchronization scan channel
3983: 
3984: ###### 3.3.1.5.1. Overview
3985: 
3986: In order to receive packets sent on the CPB logical transport, a device must first obtain information about the timing and frequency channels of those packets. If a device misses a Coarse Clock Adjustment notification, it needs to recover the current piconet clock. The synchronization scan channel is provided for these purposes. A scanning device listens for synchronization train packets on the synchronization scan channel. Once a synchronization train packet is received, the device may stop listening for synchronization train packets because it has the timing and frequency information necessary to start receiving packets sent on the CPB logical transport or to recover the piconet clock.
3987: 
3988: ###### 3.3.1.5.2. Characteristics
3989: 
3990: The synchronization scan channel uses an access code derived from the Bluetooth Device Address of the synchronization train transmitter to identify synchronization train packets on the channel. Once a synchronization train packet is received, the scanning BR/EDR Controller may start receiving packets sent on the CPB logical transport, depending on the needs of the Host and any applicable profile(s).
3991: 
3992: ###### 3.3.1.5.3. Topology
3993: 
3994: The topology formed during this scan is transient and point-to-multipoint. There can be an unlimited number of scanning devices simultaneously receiving synchronization train packets from the same synchronization train transmitter.
3995: 
3996: ###### 3.3.1.5.4. Supported layers
3997: 
3998: There is a one-way flow of packets from the synchronization train transmitting device to the scanning device(s). This may be considered a temporary physical link that exists only until the scanning device receives the required information. No further architectural layers are considered to be supported.

4000: ###### 3.3.2. LE physical channels
4001: 
4002: In the LE core system, two Bluetooth devices use a shared physical channel for communication. To achieve this, their transceivers need to be tuned to the same PHY frequency at the same time, and they need to be within a nominal range of each other.
4003: 
4004: Given that the number of PHY channels is limited, and many Bluetooth devices can be operating independently within the same spatial and temporal area, there is a strong likelihood of two pairs of independent Bluetooth devices having their transceivers tuned to the same PHY channel, resulting in a collision. Unlike BR/EDR, where an access code is used to identify the piconet, LE uses a randomly generated Access Address to identify a physical channel between devices. In the event that two devices happen to share the same PHY channel in the same area, the targeted device Access Address is used as a correlator to determine to which device the communication is directed.
4005: 
4006: Five LE physical channels are defined. Each is optimized and used for a different purpose. The LE piconet physical channel is used for communication between connected devices and is associated with a specific piconet. The LE advertising physical channel is used for broadcasting advertisements to LE devices. These advertisements can be used to discover, connect, or send user data to scanner or initiator devices. The periodic physical channel is used to send user data to scanner devices in periodic advertisements at a specified interval. The LE isochronous physical channel is used to transfer isochronous data between LE devices in an LE piconet or to transfer isochronous data between unconnected LE devices. The LE Channel Sounding physical channel carries security-related information, as well as content used for the purpose of measuring the time, phase, and amplitude of the communication channel between two LE devices in an LE piconet. 
4007: 
4008: An LE device can only use one of these LE physical channels at any given time. In order to support multiple concurrent operations the device uses time-division multiplexing between the channels. In this way a Bluetooth device can appear to support connected devices while simultaneously sending advertising broadcasts.
4009: 
4010: Whenever an LE device is synchronized to the timing and frequency of the physical channel it is said to be connected or synchronized to this channel (whether or not it is actively involved in communications over the channel). The Bluetooth specification assumes that a device is only capable of connecting to one physical channel at a time. Advanced devices may be capable of connecting or synchronizing simultaneously to more than one physical channel, but the specification does not make this assumption.
4011: 
4012: Packets on both the LE piconet physical channel and the LE advertisement broadcast channel can contain a Constant Tone Extension that can be used for the purpose of direction finding.

#### 3. 传输架构

蓝牙数据传输系统遵循分层架构。本描述介绍了蓝牙系统，包括直至并包含 L2CAP 信道在内的蓝牙核心传输层。所有蓝牙工作模式都遵循相同的通用传输架构，如[图 3.1](architecture.html#UUID-3189feb9-4465-ee4a-d054-c1cbd98f3e3f_figure-idm4568343564201633540292615318 "Figure 3.1: Bluetooth generic data transport architecture")所示。

![Bluetooth generic data transport architecture](../image/img-7db79712c93d681c79b67781d243f280.png)

图 3.1：蓝牙通用数据传输架构

  
  
  

出于效率和兼容性原因，蓝牙传输架构对逻辑层进行了细分，区分逻辑链路（logical link）和逻辑传输（logical transport）。这种细分提供了逻辑链路的通用（且通常被理解的）概念，即在两个或多个设备之间提供独立的传输。逻辑传输子层用于描述某些逻辑链路类型之间的相互依赖关系（主要是由于遗留行为的原因）。

ACL、SCO 和 eSCO 连接被视为逻辑传输，但通常表现为独立的物理链路。然而，由于它们共享使用 LT_ADDR 和确认/重复请求（ARQ）机制等资源，它们并不如期望的那样独立。因此，该架构无法用单个传输层来表示这些逻辑传输。额外的逻辑传输层在一定程度上描述了这种行为。

##### 3.1. 核心业务承载

蓝牙核心系统提供了若干标准业务承载，用于传输服务协议和应用数据。这些如以下[图 3.2](architecture.html#UUID-eed29331-57a3-2de7-c147-bd2fa23add03_figure-idm4642746768408033541876932625 "Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers")所示（为了便于表示，图中较高层在左侧，较低层在右侧）。

![Bluetooth traffic bearers](../image/img-72b45c5848b218c7c67eed25df832a27.png)

图 3.2：蓝牙业务承载

  
  
  

应用可用的核心业务承载在[图 3.2](architecture.html#UUID-eed29331-57a3-2de7-c147-bd2fa23add03_figure-idm4642746768408033541876932625 "Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers")中以带阴影的圆角矩形显示。定义为提供这些服务的架构层在[第 2 节](architecture.html#UUID-37039e1f-e0cd-37ce-2cf0-15dd6e6cff2e "2  Core system architecture")中描述。图左侧显示了多种数据业务类型，并与通常适合传输该类数据业务的业务承载相连接。

逻辑链路使用相关逻辑传输的名称和一个表示所传输数据类型的后缀来命名。（C 表示承载 LMP 或 LL 消息的控制链路，U 表示承载用户数据（L2CAP PDU）的 L2CAP 链路，S 表示承载未格式化同步或等时数据的流链路。）通常可以在不引入歧义的情况下从逻辑链路名称中省略后缀，因此对默认 ACL 逻辑传输的引用，在讨论 LMP 协议时可解析为 ACL-C 逻辑链路，在讨论 LL 协议时可解析为 LE-C 逻辑链路，在讨论 L2CAP 层时可解析为 ACL-U 或 LE-U 逻辑链路。

[图 3.2](architecture.html#UUID-eed29331-57a3-2de7-c147-bd2fa23add03_figure-idm4642746768408033541876932625 "Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers")中应用业务类型到蓝牙核心业务承载的映射，是基于将业务特征与承载特征相匹配。建议使用这些映射，因为它们为传输具有给定特征的数据提供了最自然和高效的方法。

然而，应用（或蓝牙核心系统的实现）可以选择使用不同的业务承载，或不同的映射以实现类似的结果。例如，在只有一个外围设备（Peripheral）的 BR/EDR 微微网中，中心设备（Central）可以选择通过 ACL-U 逻辑链路而不是 APB-U 逻辑链路传输 L2CAP 广播。这在带宽方面可能更高效（如果物理信道质量未严重下降）。只有在保持应用业务类型特征的情况下，使用[图 3.2](architecture.html#UUID-eed29331-57a3-2de7-c147-bd2fa23add03_figure-idm4642746768408033541876932625 "Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers")中替代传输路径才是可接受的。

[图 3.2](architecture.html#UUID-eed29331-57a3-2de7-c147-bd2fa23add03_figure-idm4642746768408033541876932625 "Figure 3.2: Bluetooth traffic bearers")显示了多种应用业务类型。这些用于对可提交给蓝牙核心系统的数据类型进行分类。如果中间过程修改了原始数据业务类型，则原始数据业务类型可能与提交给蓝牙核心系统的类型不同。例如，视频数据以恒定速率生成，但中间编码过程可能将其改变为可变速率，例如通过 MPEG4 编码。对于蓝牙核心系统而言，仅关注所提交数据的特征。

###### 3.1.1. 成帧数据业务

L2CAP 层服务为异步和等时用户数据提供面向帧的传输。应用以可变大小的帧（不超过该信道协商的最大值）向该服务提交数据，这些帧以相同的形式交付给远端设备上的对应应用。不要求应用向数据中插入额外的成帧信息，但如果需要，应用可以这样做（此类成帧对蓝牙核心系统是不可见的）。

可创建面向连接的 L2CAP 信道，用于在两个蓝牙设备之间传输单播（点对点）数据。面向连接的信道提供了一个上下文，在该上下文中可对信道上传输的数据应用特定属性。例如，可应用服务质量参数或流控和差错控制模式。面向连接的 L2CAP 信道使用 L2CAP 连接过程创建。

存在无连接 BR/EDR L2CAP 信道，用于广播数据或传输单播数据。在微微网拓扑中，中心设备（Central）始终是广播数据的源，外围设备（Peripheral）是接收者。无连接 L2CAP 信道上的广播业务是单向的。在无连接 L2CAP 信道上发送的单播数据可以是单向或双向的。在 L2CAP 无连接信道上发送的单播数据提供了一种替代机制，可以发送与在基本模式下运行的 L2CAP 面向连接信道具有相同可靠性级别的数据，而无需承担打开 L2CAP 面向连接信道所产生的额外时延。不支持 LE L2CAP 无连接信道。

BR/EDR L2CAP 信道具有关联的 QoS 设置，该设置定义了对数据帧交付的约束。这些 QoS 设置可用于指示（例如）数据是等时的，因此具有有限的生命周期，超过该生命周期后变为无效；或者数据应在给定时间段内交付；或者数据是可靠的，应无差错地交付，无论耗时多长。

一些 L2CAP 信道是在建立 ACL-U 和/或 LE-U 逻辑链路时创建的固定信道。这些固定信道具有固定的信道标识符和固定配置，并且不允许在创建后协商配置。这些固定信道用于 BR/EDR 和 LE L2CAP 信令（ACL-U 或 LE-U）、无连接信道（ACL-U 和 APB-U）、安全管理器协议（Security Manager Protocol，LE-U）以及属性协议（Attribute Protocol，ACL-U 或 LE-U）。

L2CAP 信道管理器负责安排在适当的基带逻辑链路上传输 L2CAP 信道数据帧，可能将其与具有类似特征的其他 L2CAP 信道复用到该基带逻辑链路上。

###### 3.1.2. 非成帧数据业务

如果应用不需要以帧的形式交付数据，可能因为其包含流内成帧，或因为数据是纯流，则可以避免使用 L2CAP 信道，而直接使用基带逻辑链路。

蓝牙核心系统支持使用 SCO-S 或 eSCO-S 逻辑链路直接传输等时且恒定速率（对于预成帧数据为比特率或帧率）的应用数据。这些逻辑链路预留物理信道带宽，并提供锁定到微微网时钟的恒定速率传输。数据以固定大小的分组在固定间隔传输，这两个参数均在信道建立期间协商。eSCO 链路提供更多比特率选择，并通过在出错时使用有限重传提供更高的可靠性。eSCO 支持增强数据速率（EDR）操作，但 SCO 逻辑传输不支持。SCO 和 eSCO 逻辑传输不支持复用逻辑链路或蓝牙核心内的任何进一步分层。应用可以选择在所提交的 SCO/eSCO 流内对若干流进行分层，前提是所提交的流是或具有恒定速率流的外观。

蓝牙核心系统还支持使用配置文件广播数据（Profile Broadcast Data，PBD）逻辑链路直接传输应用数据。该逻辑链路类似于 SCO-S 和 eSCO-S，因为它预留物理信道带宽，提供锁定到微微网时钟的恒定速率传输，并以固定间隔传输数据。它不支持复用逻辑链路或蓝牙核心内的任何进一步分层，但与 SCO-S 和 eSCO-S 不同，它支持从单个发射机向多个接收机广播数据。

应用从基带可用的逻辑链路中选择最合适的类型，并创建和配置它以传输数据流，完成后释放它。（应用通常还使用成帧 L2CAP 单播信道将其 C-plane 信息传输给远端设备上的对等应用。）

如果应用数据是等时的且为可变速率，则只能由 L2CAP 单播信道承载，因此将作为成帧数据处理。

LE 系统不支持非成帧数据业务。

###### 3.1.3. 业务承载的可靠性

如果接收机能够检测所接收分组中的错误并请求重传直到错误消除，则该链路或信道被表征为可靠的。这称为自动重复请求（Automatic Repeat reQuest，ARQ）机制。由于所使用的差错检测系统，接收数据中可能仍残留一些未检测到的错误。这些错误发生的速率取决于差错检测系统的细节。

如果接收机不能检测所接收分组中的错误，或者能检测错误但不能请求重传，则该链路或信道被表征为不可靠的。在后一种情况下（如大多数广播链路），接收机传递给较高层的分组可能没有错误，但不能保证所有发送的分组都被接收到。不可靠链路的用途通常依赖于提高传输冗余度的技术，例如使用前向纠错或在数据有效时从较高层重复数据，以增加接收机成功接收至少一个副本的概率。

###### 3.1.3.1. BR/EDR 可靠性

蓝牙是一种无线通信系统。在恶劣的射频（RF）环境中，该系统应被视为固有不可靠。为了抵消这一点，系统在每一层提供保护级别。基带分组头使用前向纠错（FEC）编码以允许接收机进行纠错，并使用头错误校验（HEC）来检测纠错后残留的错误。某些基带分组类型对有效载荷包含 FEC。此外，一些基带分组类型包含循环冗余差错校验（CRC）。

在 ACL 逻辑传输上，差错检测算法的结果用于驱动简单的 ARQ 协议。这通过重传未通过接收机差错校验算法的分组来提供增强的可靠性。可以修改此机制以支持时延敏感的分组，方法是在分组的有用寿命已过期时，在发射机处丢弃未成功传输的分组。eSCO 链路使用此机制的修改版本，通过允许有限次数的重传来提高可靠性。

通过此 ARQ 机制获得的可靠性仅取决于 HEC 和 CRC 码检测错误的能力。在大多数情况下这是足够的，但已经表明，对于较长的分组类型，未检测到错误的概率过高，无法支持典型应用，特别是那些传输大量数据的应用。

L2CAP 层提供了额外的差错控制级别，旨在检测基带未检测到的偶发错误并请求重传受影响的数据。这提供了典型蓝牙应用所需的可靠性级别。所产生的残留错误速率与其他通信系统中的速率相当。

发射机可能从发送队列中移除分组，使得接收机不能接收到序列中的所有分组。如果发生这种情况，缺失分组的检测被委托给 L2CAP 层。

流链路具有介于可靠链路和不可靠链路之间的可靠性特征，具体取决于当前的工作条件。

###### 3.1.3.2. LE 可靠性

与 BR/EDR 一样，在恶劣的射频环境中，LE 系统应被视为固有不可靠。为了抵消这一点，系统在每一层提供保护级别。LL 分组使用 24 位循环冗余差错校验（CRC）来覆盖分组有效载荷的内容。如果分组有效载荷的 CRC 校验失败，接收机不对该分组进行确认，发送方将重传该分组。

由于与 BR/EDR 相比 CRC 更长且典型消息更短，L2CAP 层无需提供单独的差错检测和重传机制。

对于数据物理信道 PDU，PDU 头包含逻辑链路标识符（LLID）、下一个期望序列号（NESN）、序列号（SN）、更多数据（MD）、CTEInfo 存在（CP）、有效载荷长度，并可能包含 CTEInfo。对于包含控制命令的数据物理信道 PDU，数据信道 PDU 有效载荷包含命令操作码和特定于该命令的控制数据。有一个可选的消息完整性校验（MIC）值用于认证数据 PDU。对于作为数据的数据物理信道 PDU，数据物理信道 PDU 有效载荷包含 L2CAP 数据。

等时物理信道 PDU 可以是连接等时 PDU 或广播等时 PDU。连接等时 PDU 包含一个头并可能包含等时有效载荷。头字段包含逻辑链路标识符（LLID）、序列号（SN）、下一个期望序列号（NESN）、关闭等时事件（CIE）、空 PDU 指示（NPI）和有效载荷长度。连接等时 PDU 还可能包含消息完整性校验（MIC）字段。

广播等时 PDU 包含一个头以及等时数据或控制数据。头字段包含逻辑链路标识符（LLID）、控制子事件序列号（CSSN）、控制子事件传输标志（CSTF）和有效载荷长度。广播等时 PDU 还可能包含消息完整性校验（MIC）字段。

广播物理信道分组和数据物理信道分组都可以包含恒定音扩展，可用于确定所接收射频信号的相对方向。

##### 3.3. 物理信道

定义了多种类型的物理信道。所有蓝牙物理信道的特征是一组 PHY 频率结合时间参数，并受空间因素限制。对于基本微微网物理信道和自适应微微网物理信道，使用跳频定期改变频率，以减少干扰的影响并出于法规原因。

蓝牙 BR/EDR 系统和 LE 系统在使用物理信道的方式上略有不同。

###### 3.3.1. BR/EDR 物理信道

在 BR/EDR 核心系统中，对等设备使用共享的物理信道进行通信。为此，它们的收发器需要同时调谐到相同的 PHY 频率，并且它们需要在彼此的标称范围内。

鉴于射频载波数量有限，且许多蓝牙设备可能在同一空间和时间区域内独立运行，两个独立的蓝牙设备的收发器很可能调谐到相同的射频载波，从而导致物理信道冲突。为减轻此冲突的不良影响，物理信道上的每次传输都以一个接入码开始，该接入码被调谐到该物理信道的设备用作相关码。此信道接入码是物理信道的属性。接入码存在于每个传输分组的开始处。

定义了若干 BR/EDR 物理信道。每个都经过优化并用于不同目的。其中两个物理信道（基本微微网信道和自适应微微网信道）用于连接设备之间的通信，并与特定微微网相关联。其他 BR/EDR 物理信道用于发现（查询扫描信道）和连接（寻呼扫描信道）蓝牙设备。同步扫描物理信道被设备用于获取有关无连接外围广播物理链路的时序和频率信息，或恢复当前的微微网时钟。

蓝牙设备在任何给定时间只能使用一个 BR/EDR 物理信道。为了支持多个并发操作，设备在信道之间使用时分复用。这样，蓝牙设备可以看似同时在多个微微网中运行，同时还可被发现和连接。

当蓝牙设备同步到物理信道的时序、频率和接入码时，称该设备"连接"到此信道（无论其是否积极参与该信道上的通信）。蓝牙规范假设设备在任何时间只能连接到一个物理信道。高级设备可能能够同时连接到多个物理信道，但规范不假设这是可能的。

###### 3.3.1.1. 基本微微网信道

###### 3.3.1.1.1. 概述

基本微微网信道用于正常运行期间连接设备之间的通信。

###### 3.3.1.1.2. 特征

基本微微网信道的特征是遍历 PHY 信道的伪随机跳频序列。该跳频序列对于微微网是唯一的，由中心设备（Central）的蓝牙设备地址确定。跳频序列中的相位由中心设备的蓝牙时钟确定。参与微微网的所有蓝牙设备都在时间和跳频上同步到该信道。

该信道被划分为时隙，每个时隙对应一个 PHY 跳频频率。连续的跳频对应不同的 PHY 跳频频率。时隙根据微微网中心设备的蓝牙时钟编号。参与微微网的蓝牙设备传输的分组对齐到时隙边界开始。每个分组以信道接入码开始，该接入码由微微网中心设备的蓝牙设备地址导出。

在基本微微网信道上，中心设备控制对信道的访问。中心设备仅在偶数时隙开始其传输。中心设备传输的分组与时隙起始对齐，并定义微微网时序。中心设备传输的分组最多可占用五个时隙，具体取决于分组类型。

中心设备的每次传输都是携带某一逻辑传输信息的分组。外围设备可以在物理信道上响应传输。响应的特征由所寻址的逻辑传输定义。

例如，在异步面向连接逻辑传输（ACL）上，被寻址的外围设备通过传输包含相同逻辑传输信息的分组来响应，该分组名义上与下一个（奇数）时隙起始对齐。此类分组最多可占用五个时隙，具体取决于分组类型。在广播逻辑传输上，不允许任何外围设备响应。

###### 3.3.1.1.3. 拓扑

基本微微网信道可由任意数量的蓝牙设备共享，仅受微微网中心设备上可用资源的限制。只有一个设备是微微网中心设备，所有其他设备都是微微网外围设备。所有通信都在中心设备和外围设备之间进行。在微微网信道上，外围设备之间没有直接通信。

然而，微微网内可支持的逻辑传输数量存在限制。这意味着，尽管共享信道的蓝牙设备数量没有理论限制，但可以积极参与与中心设备交换数据的这些设备的数量是有限的。

###### 3.3.1.1.4. 支持的层

基本微微网信道支持若干用于通用通信的物理链路、逻辑传输、逻辑链路和 L2CAP 信道。

###### 3.3.1.2. 自适应微微网信道

###### 3.3.1.2.1. 概述

自适应微微网信道与基本微微网信道在两个方面不同。首先，外围设备传输所用的频率与其中心设备在前一次传输中使用的频率相同。换言之，中心设备和后续外围设备分组之间的频率不重新计算。其次，自适应微微网信道可基于少于全部 79 个频率。跳频图案中的一些频率可以通过标记为"未使用"而被省略。其余的 79 个频率被包括在内。两个序列相同，只是每当基本伪随机跳频序列选择了一个未使用的频率时，它被从已使用集合中选择的替代频率替换。所使用的频率集合在同一自适应微微网信道上的不同物理链路之间可能不同。

由于自适应微微网信道使用与基本微微网信道相同的时序和接入码，两个信道上的物理链路通常重合。这提供了一个有意的好处，因为它允许基本微微网信道或自适应微微网信道中的外围设备调整其与中心设备的同步。

自适应微微网物理信道的拓扑和支持的层与基本微微网物理信道相同，但有一个例外：在自适应微微网物理信道上，单个中心设备可以使用单个 CPB 逻辑传输向无限数量的外围设备传输数据。然而，在这种情况下，数据仅从中心设备传输到外围设备，而不是从外围设备传输到中心设备。

###### 3.3.1.3. 查询扫描信道

###### 3.3.1.3.1. 概述

为了使设备能被发现，使用查询扫描信道。可发现设备在其查询扫描信道上侦听查询请求，然后对该请求发送响应。为了使设备能发现其他设备，它以伪随机方式遍历（跳频）所有可能的查询扫描信道频率，在每个频率上发送查询请求并侦听任何响应。

###### 3.3.1.3.2. 特征

查询扫描信道遵循较慢的跳频图案，并使用接入码来区分使用不同物理信道的两个同址设备偶尔占用相同无线电频率的情况。

查询扫描信道上使用的接入码取自所有蓝牙设备共享的预留查询接入码集合。一个接入码用于一般查询，若干附加接入码预留用于有限查询。每个设备可访问多个不同的查询扫描信道。由于所有这些信道共享相同的跳频图案，如果设备能够同时相关多个接入码，则它可以同时占用多个查询扫描信道。

使用其某个查询扫描信道的设备在该信道上保持被动，直到它从另一个蓝牙设备接收到此信道上的查询消息。这由适当的查询接入码识别。然后，查询扫描设备将遵循查询响应过程向查询设备返回响应。

为了使设备能发现其他蓝牙设备，它使用查询扫描信道发送查询请求。由于它没有要发现设备的先验知识，因此无法知道查询扫描信道的确切特征。

该设备利用了查询扫描信道具有较少跳频频率和较慢跳频速率这一事实。查询设备在每个查询扫描跳频频率上发送查询请求并侦听查询响应。传输以较快的速率进行，使查询设备能够在相当短的时间段内覆盖所有查询扫描频率。

###### 3.3.1.3.3. 拓扑

查询设备和可发现设备使用简单的分组交换来完成查询功能。在此事务期间形成的拓扑是简单且瞬时的点对点连接。

###### 3.3.1.3.4. 支持的层

在查询设备和可发现设备之间交换分组期间，可以认为这些设备之间存在临时物理链路。然而，这个概念相当无关紧要，因为它没有物理表示，而只是由设备之间的简短事务所隐含。不考虑支持进一步的架构层。

###### 3.3.1.4. 寻呼扫描信道

###### 3.3.1.4.1. 概述

可连接设备（准备接受连接的设备）使用寻呼扫描信道来实现连接。可连接设备在其寻呼扫描信道上侦听寻呼请求，一旦收到，就与该设备进入一系列交换。为了使设备能连接到另一个设备，它以伪随机方式遍历（跳频）所有寻呼扫描信道频率，在每个频率上发送寻呼请求并侦听响应。

###### 3.3.1.4.2. 特征

寻呼扫描信道使用从扫描设备的蓝牙设备地址导出的接入码来识别信道上的通信。寻呼扫描信道使用比基本微微网信道和自适应微微网信道的跳频速率更慢的跳频速率。跳频选择算法使用扫描设备的蓝牙设备时钟作为输入。

使用其寻呼扫描信道的设备保持被动，直到它从另一个蓝牙设备接收到寻呼请求。这由寻呼扫描信道接入码识别。然后两个设备将遵循寻呼过程形成连接。在寻呼过程成功完成后，两个设备都切换到基本微微网信道，该信道的特征是以寻呼设备作为中心设备。

为了使设备能连接到另一个蓝牙设备，它使用目标设备的寻呼扫描信道来发送寻呼请求。如果寻呼设备不知道目标设备的寻呼扫描信道的相位，因此也不知道目标设备的当前跳频频率。寻呼设备在每个寻呼扫描跳频频率上发送寻呼请求并侦听寻呼响应。这以较快的跳频速率进行，使寻呼设备能够在相当短的时间段内覆盖所有寻呼扫描频率。

寻呼设备可能对目标设备的蓝牙时钟有所了解（在两个设备之间先前的事务中指示，或由于先前与该设备一起参与微微网的结果），在这种情况下，它能够预测目标设备寻呼扫描信道的相位。它可以使用此信息来优化寻呼和寻呼扫描过程的同步，并加快连接的形成。

###### 3.3.1.4.3. 拓扑

寻呼设备和可连接设备使用简单的分组交换来完成寻呼功能。在此事务期间形成的拓扑是简单且瞬时的点对点连接。

###### 3.3.1.4.4. 支持的层

在寻呼设备和可连接设备之间交换分组期间，可以认为这些设备之间存在临时物理链路。然而，这个概念相当无关紧要，因为它没有物理表示，而只是由设备之间的简短事务所隐含。不考虑支持进一步的架构层。

###### 3.3.1.5. 同步扫描信道

###### 3.3.1.5.1. 概述

为了接收在 CPB 逻辑传输上发送的分组，设备必须首先获取这些分组的时序和频率信道信息。如果设备错过了粗略时钟调整通知，它需要恢复当前的微微网时钟。同步扫描信道就是为此目的而提供的。扫描设备在同步扫描信道上侦听同步序列分组。一旦接收到同步序列分组，设备就可以停止侦听同步序列分组，因为它已具有开始接收在 CPB 逻辑传输上发送的分组或恢复微微网时钟所需的时序和频率信息。

###### 3.3.1.5.2. 特征

同步扫描信道使用从同步序列发射机的蓝牙设备地址导出的接入码来识别信道上的同步序列分组。一旦接收到同步序列分组，扫描的 BR/EDR 控制器（Controller）可以根据主机（Host）和任何适用配置文件的需要开始接收在 CPB 逻辑传输上发送的分组。

###### 3.3.1.5.3. 拓扑

在此扫描期间形成的拓扑是瞬时的且为点到多点。可以有无限数量的扫描设备同时接收来自同一同步序列发射机的同步序列分组。

###### 3.3.1.5.4. 支持的层

存在从同步序列发射设备到扫描设备的单向分组流。这可以被认为是一个仅存在到扫描设备接收到所需信息为止的临时物理链路。不考虑支持进一步的架构层。

###### 3.3.2. LE 物理信道

在 LE 核心系统中，两个蓝牙设备使用共享的物理信道进行通信。为此，它们的收发器需要同时调谐到相同的 PHY 频率，并且它们需要在彼此的标称范围内。

鉴于 PHY 信道数量有限，且许多蓝牙设备可能在同一空间和时间区域内独立运行，两对独立的蓝牙设备的收发器很可能调谐到相同的 PHY 信道，从而导致冲突。与使用接入码识别微微网的 BR/EDR 不同，LE 使用随机生成的接入地址来识别设备之间的物理信道。如果两个设备碰巧在同一区域共享相同的 PHY 信道，则使用目标设备的接入地址作为相关器来确定通信定向到哪个设备。

定义了五种 LE 物理信道。每种都经过优化并用于不同目的。LE 微微网物理信道用于连接设备之间的通信，并与特定微微网相关联。LE 广播物理信道用于向 LE 设备广播广播信息。这些广播可用于发现、连接或向扫描者或发起者设备发送用户数据。周期性物理信道用于在周期性广播中以指定间隔向扫描者设备发送用户数据。LE 等时物理信道用于在 LE 微微网中的 LE 设备之间传输等时数据，或在未连接的 LE 设备之间传输等时数据。LE 信道探测（CS）物理信道承载与安全相关的信息，以及用于测量 LE 微微网中两个 LE 设备之间通信信道的时间、相位和振幅的内容。 

LE 设备在任何给定时间只能使用这些 LE 物理信道中的一个。为了支持多个并发操作，设备在信道之间使用时分复用。这样，蓝牙设备可以看似支持连接的设备，同时发送广播。

当 LE 设备同步到物理信道的时序和频率时，称该设备连接或同步到此信道（无论其是否积极参与该信道上的通信）。蓝牙规范假设设备在任何时间只能连接到一个物理信道。高级设备可能能够同时连接或同步到多个物理信道，但规范不做出此假设。

LE 微微网物理信道和 LE 广播信道上的分组都可以包含恒定音扩展，可用于测向目的。

###### 3.3.2.1. LE 微微网物理信道

###### 3.3.2.1.1. 概述

LE 微微网物理信道用于正常运行期间连接的 LE 设备之间的通信。

###### 3.3.2.1.2. 特征

LE 微微网物理信道的特征是接入地址、PHY 信道的伪随机序列以及中心设备提供的三个附加参数。第一个是信道图，指示微微网中使用的 PHY 信道集合。第二个是用作完整 PHY 信道集合索引的伪随机数。第三个是中心设备在连接请求之后发送第一个数据分组的时序。

该信道被划分为连接事件，每个连接事件对应一个 PHY 跳频信道。连续的连接事件对应不同的 PHY 跳频信道。中心设备在连接建立之后发送的第一个分组为所有未来连接事件的时序设定锚点。在连接事件中，中心设备向微微网中的外围设备传输分组，外围设备可以用自己的分组响应。

在 LE 微微网物理信道上，中心设备控制对信道的访问。中心设备在定期发生的连接事件中开始其传输。中心设备传输的分组与连接事件起始对齐，并定义微微网时序。

中心设备的每次传输都包含携带某一逻辑传输信息的分组。外围设备可以在物理信道上响应传输。

LE 微微网物理信道类似于 BR/EDR 自适应微微网信道，因为使用的 PHY 信道集合可以修改以避免干扰。信道图中使用的信道集合由中心设备在连接建立期间确定。在连接期间，中心设备可以在必要时更改信道图以避免新的干扰源。外围设备可以向中心设备提供信道分类信息。

有 37 个 LE 微微网信道。中心设备可以通过指示已使用信道的信道图减少此数量。当跳频图案命中未使用的信道时，未使用的信道被已使用信道集合中的替代信道替换。LE 微微网物理信道可以使用任何 LE PHY。

###### 3.3.2.1.3. 拓扑

LE 微微网物理信道由恰好两个 LE 设备共享。

LE 设备一次可以属于一个或多个微微网，即 LE 设备可以是零个或多个微微网中的外围设备，也可以是零个或多个微微网中的中心设备。

在两个 LE 设备身份或不可解析私有地址之间只能存在一个 LE 微微网物理信道。

###### 3.3.2.1.4. 支持的层

LE 微微网物理信道支持用于通用通信的 L2CAP 信道。

###### 3.3.2.2. 广播物理信道

###### 3.3.2.2.1. 概述

LE 广播物理信道用于在两个设备之间建立连接，或在未连接的设备之间通信广播信息。
